items.toString:
*WHAT*

Define job stories, user narratives, and goals for this [epic brief|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1lue9gfJ15rcGLC3QRVSIXGamGL04VSfPCspscPvG510/edit#heading=h.2ac01bg8eck9].

 

*HOW*

For this task, the UX designer should:
 * Gather requirements and/or user needs from relevant stakeholders.
 * Define job stories, user narratives, goals, etc.
 * Conduct a workshop session with all relevant (or interested) stakeholders to brainstorm ideas/solutions for the job stories. This would also help to flesh out any already documented details.
 * Extract insights from the workshop.
 * Fill out the epic brief.
 * Review the document with stakeholders including the UX team, engineering, and BU.
 * Make any further changes as required.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * All necessary sections of the epic brief document have been filled out.
 * UX team, engineering, and BU review and acceptance.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

When I manage access to a service registry instance, I want to select which user or service accounts can access the resources at the group-level so that I have fine-grained control and I am able to 
 * allow certain users from accessing resources in the instance and comply with security requirements
 * block certain users from accessing resources in the instance and comply with security requirements
 * grant permissions (such as read/write) to users to limit access to certain group-level resources


 

*HOW*

For this proposed enhancement, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options and create UX mockups for them. 
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

The following steps should be adhered to:
 * The final, proposed design ideas must align with PatternFly design components.
 * When sharing final design details, include links to all PF components used in designs, describe component behavior in the context of the use case. Also, include the final microcopy if needed.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

We want to link API Designer from RHOSAK’s Topic details UI to allow users to create and edit topic schemas. 

 

*HOW*
 * Under the Schemas tab in the Topic details view, the user can select a Service Registry instance. If the system finds the matching schema(s), the user will be able to view and edit it using API Designer. Otherwise, they can create or import a schema, edit it using API Designer, and register it in RHOSR. 
 * The user flow for these use cases is seamless i.e. the user doesn’t have to switch back and forth between RHOSAK and RHOAD to edit, create, or import schemas. However, there is an option via the editor view to go to the API Designer UI. 
 * A few other action items in the Schemas tab UI allow the user to go to the SR instance (artifact list view) and view schema details in RHOSR (artifact details view).
 * Design mockups for this task are available here: [https://www.figma.com/proto/BswZf9XbyY1VOTHAdUOUgx/API-Designer?node-id=4356%3A73912&scaling=min-zoom&page-id=0%3A1&starting-point-node-id=4356%3A73912]

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Versioning of content.*

We want to support simple versioning of Designs. Versioning of a design is simply giving a user-provided name to a specific iteration of the design content. Once a version is tagged, it cannot be changed (it is immutable).

Versions can be supported in both Phase 1 and in Phase 2. We will need to decide if it’s worth pursuing basic versioning in Phase 1 or simply wait for Phase 2.

 

*Phase 1 (extended)*

We do not currently save more than one version of a design in phase 1 of API Designer. Each time the user clicks the “Save” button in the editor, the content is overwritten. However, we could easily make a change to start tracking multiple versions. We could have an action in the UI that allowed the user to tag the current version of the design with a name, and then persist that copy in the browser database.

This would then allow the user to, for example, revert back to an older version of their design. It would also allow the user to compare two versions for differences, or compare the current version with a previously tagged version.

 

*Phase 2*

The phase 2 approach to versioning is, I think, the same. The only difference is that the content being tagged is stored on the server, and the versions of each design are then available to all users in the organization.

The act of versioning a design in phase 2 also represents an “event” that can be used to trigger automations/integrations.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options for the Phase 1 approach (keeping in mind that we will migrate these designs to phase 2 i.e. with backend functionality) and create UX mockups for it. 
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.


 * Explore how the designs can be migrated with phase 2 approach.
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

The following steps should be adhered to:
 * The final, proposed design ideas must align with PatternFly design components.
 * When sharing final design details, include links to all PF components used in designs, describe component behavior in the context of the use case. Also, include final microcopy if needed.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Code generation - client SDKs/server stubs.*

Once users have created and edited designs in API Designer, they will want to do something with those designs. One obvious example of this is the ability to generate server stubs and client SDKs. Examples of this include the ability to generate a Quarkus-compatible set of JAX-RS interfaces and data types from an OpenAPI document, and also the ability to generate a Node.js client SDK from the same.

Code generation is broadly useful, and we should consider implementing it for Phase 1. The feature likely looks a bit different in Phase 1 vs. Phase 2.

 

*Phase 1 (extended)*

This could be a simple action sitting alongside “Download design” and “Export to RHOSR”. The “Generate Code” action could prompt the user for some details and then perform the code generation. The result would be a ZIP file containing the generated code.

 

*Phase 2*

In phase 2, I think Code Generation should be one of the integrations we support (see the section on Integration below).

Having code generation as an integration allows us to better automate it based on interesting events that could happen in the phase 2 server.  For example, whenever an API Designer is tagged as a new “version”, the server stubs could be automatically generated and pushed to Git.

Code generation does require a server component, but perhaps it can be developed and deployed as a standalone component.  This could speed up the development time and result in a service that might be broadly useful across multiple MAS projects.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options for the Phase 1 approach (keeping in mind that we will migrate these designs to phase 2 i.e. with backend functionality) and create UX mockups for it. 
 ** Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.
 * Explore how the designs can be migrated with phase 2 approach.
 ** Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.

*Guidelines*

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Code generation - client SDKs/server stubs.*

Once users have created and edited designs in API Designer, they will want to do something with those designs. One obvious example of this is the ability to generate server stubs and client SDKs. Examples of this include the ability to generate a Quarkus-compatible set of JAX-RS interfaces and data types from an OpenAPI document, and also the ability to generate a Node.js client SDK from the same.

Code generation is broadly useful, and we should consider implementing it for Phase 1. The feature likely looks a bit different in Phase 1 vs. Phase 2.

 

*Phase 1 (extended)*

This could be a simple action sitting alongside “Download design” and “Export to RHOSR”. The “Generate Code” action could prompt the user for some details and then perform the code generation. The result would be a ZIP file containing the generated code.

 

*Phase 2*

In phase 2, I think Code Generation should be one of the integrations we support (see the section on Integration below).

Having code generation as an integration allows us to better automate it based on interesting events that could happen in the phase 2 server.  For example, whenever an API Designer is tagged as a new “version”, the server stubs could be automatically generated and pushed to Git.

Code generation does require a server component, but perhaps it can be developed and deployed as a standalone component.  This could speed up the development time and result in a service that might be broadly useful across multiple MAS projects.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options for the Phase 1 approach (keeping in mind that we will migrate these designs to phase 2 i.e. with backend functionality) and create UX mockups for it. 
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.


 * Explore how the designs can be migrated with phase 2 approach.
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

The following steps should be adhered to:
 * The final, proposed design ideas must align with PatternFly design components.
 * When sharing final design details, include links to all PF components used in designs, describe component behavior in the context of the use case. Also, include final microcopy if needed.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Custom validation rules.*

A key function of the editors in API Designer is their ability to validate content in real time. The way content is validated depends on the type (Avro vs. OpenAPI for example). Going forward, an important technology for performing validation will likely be Spectral. Currently validation is handled internally by each editor. In most cases only syntax validation is performed.  For example, the Avro editor currently only checks that the content is valid JSON, it doesn’t check if the content is actually Avro (this is the difference between syntax and semantic validation).

It would be useful for users to be able to supply their own validation rules, for example using Spectral rulesets. These configured rulesets can then be used in our editors to perform customized semantic validation of content.

Similarly to template management, we could likely enable this functionality in Phase 1 and then migrate it to Phase 2. Or we could simply implement it as part of Phase 2 from the start.

 

*Phase 1 (extended)*

We could create a “Validation Rulesets” management page within API Designer that allows users to configure their own custom rulesets, likely based on Spectral. Users could manage a collection of rulesets and perhaps indicate which one is the default to be used while editing.  Rulesets would need to be configured based on the type of content. So the UI would need to allow management of a collection of rulesets for each type.

Much like with templates, we could allow users to simply configure a URL that points to a ruleset file. In this way, organizations could provide their own rulesets that their developers could simply reference in a Phase 1 API Designer. And again, we could additionally invent a “Ruleset Catalog” format that could allow organizations to configure multiple rulesets at once for easy import into each user’s API Designer.

Once the rulesets have been defined, the editor page will need a way for users to select which validation ruleset(s) they want to apply during editing.

 

*Phase 2*

Once we have a back-end server, we would want a “Validation Rulesets” management page that was accessible only by Admin level users. This page would allow admins to manage the collection of rulesets for each type, resulting in better sharing across their organization.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options for the Phase 1 approach (keeping in mind that we will migrate these designs to phase 2 i.e. with backend functionality) and create UX mockups for it. 
 ** Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Template management.*

Currently the API Designer allows users to create new designs from a blank (empty) document or (in some cases) from industry standard examples/templates. It would be an improvement if users could configure their own. We can support user-configured templates in Phase 1 immediately and then migrate that support into Phase 2.

 

*Phase 1 (extended)*

Create a “Template Management” page in the UI that allows a user to configure templates for each of the types we support (Avro, OpenAPI, JSON Schema, etc). Configuration of a template could be a simple URL to a resource of the correct format. Content found at the URL would then be used whenever the user created a new design of the right type and using the configured template.

Red Hat customers (organizations) could create a set of templates and make them available at some web location. Each of the users within the organization could then link to those templates as a way of sharing them.

Further, we could invent a “Template Catalog” index format so that an organization could create a single file that would contain a list of templates. In this way, we could make it extremely easy for organizations to develop a collection of templates that can quickly and easily be imported into an individual user’s API Designer (and thus shared across multiple developers) without the need for an API Designer back-end.

 

*Phase 2*

In Phase 2 we could consider an approach where Admin level users could manage a collection of templates that we then store in the API Designer server’s database. This would require a similar “Template Management” page (accessible only by admin users) as the one we might create in Phase 1. But instead of simply configuring a collection of URLs to template files and storing them in the browser, the admin would be uploading actual template content (with some metadata).

These templates can then be queried by non-admin users when they create new Designs, so that the templates can be selected during the creation process.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore design options for the Phase 1 approach (keeping in mind that we will migrate these designs to phase 2 i.e. with backend functionality) and create UX mockups for it. 
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.


 * Explore how the designs can be migrated with phase 2 approach.
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

*Proposed feature: Improve Avro editor.*

For each type of content we support in API Designer, we want as mature and useful an editing experience as possible. To that end, we will continue to evaluate whether we can leverage existing open source editors or improve our own. In the case of Avro, there is an open source project called “Javro” that offers an incrementally better editing experience compared with what we have today. The project can be found here: [https://github.com/javro/javro]

This editor provides improved auto-completion, Avro specific validations, and a preview panel. We should attempt to either use this project directly (if possible) or use it (both design and implementation) to inspire us to improve our current Monaco based Avro editor.

 

*HOW*

For this proposed feature, the UX designer should:
 * Explore Javro editor and compare it with currently used Monaco editor.
 * Explore if we can use this proposed editor directly
 * Review the proposed editor with PatternFly team, discuss responsiveness and accessibility concerns.

 * Can we improve current Monaco editor to include the functionalities provided by Javro?
 * Create UX mockups as needed
 * Review the findings and designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

The following steps should be adhered to:
 * The final, proposed design ideas must align with PatternFly design components.
 * When sharing final design details, include links to all PF components used in designs, describe component behavior in the context of the use case. Also, include final microcopy if needed.

The following suggestions are related to the _Getting started with the rhoas CLI for Red Hat OpenShift Service Registry_ document.

 
----
*1.  Inaccurate description of "rhoas service-registry artifact list" command*

In the [Uploading Service Registry artifacts|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_service_registry/1/guide/1630486d-c8d0-45d0-b2de-7fdb52c78499#_dbb873d7-3089-4344-bae9-1c436080b115] section, step 3 has the following text:
"This example lists all artifacts belonging to the Service Registry instance."

for the following command:
rhoas service-registry artifact list
 

However, this statement is not strictly accurate. As described in the RHOAS CLI reference ([service-registry artifact list|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_application_services/1/guide/8bd088a6-b7b7-4e5d-832a-b0f0494f9070#_5f6ed3a9-3b73-405f-a6c3-404d59af4285] section), that command lists 'all artifacts {+}for the "default" artifact group{+}'.

(It is not currently possible to list all artifacts for an instance - see the enhancement requested in MGDSR-405.)

 

We should update the lead-in text in step 3 to include a reference to the default group.

 
----
*2.  Prerequisites*

In the [Creating a Service Registry instance|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_service_registry/1/guide/1630486d-c8d0-45d0-b2de-7fdb52c78499#_09e5f9eb-a742-4307-83a0-fbe0746131a1] section, the Prequisites section has the following text:
"You're logged in to {{{}rhoas{}}}."

This prerequisite applies to _all_ of the sections in the document, but is listed only in the first one.

Would it be better to move this text to the main [Prerequisites|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_service_registry/1/guide/1630486d-c8d0-45d0-b2de-7fdb52c78499#_e8e1dde7-be5a-4ff4-9a4f-6330274fe687] section at the start of the entire document. Perhaps add this text in a second bullet point, after the bullet point about installing rhoas?

Alternatively, perhaps move it to be the first step in the first Procedure, and rephrase it as an imperative:
"In a terminal, log in to {{{}rhoas{}}}."

In either case, we should provide the login command so that the user doesn't have to open the [_Installing and configuring the rhoas CLI_|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_application_services/1/guide/bb30ee92-9e0a-4fd6-a67f-aed8910d7da3] document to find it:
$ rhoas login
{{}}
----
*3.  Code headings*

As agreed in a recent MAS-K CCS Style discussion, remove any code headings that are superfluous.

 
----

h3. WHAT

 * Service account endpoint: [https://sso.redhat.com/auth/realms/redhat-external/apis/service_accounts/v1]

 * Base URL: [https://sso.redhat.com/|https://sso.redhat.com/auth/realms/redhat-external/apis/service_accounts/v1]
 * JWKS: [https://sso.redhat.com/auth/realms/redhat-external/protocol/openid-connect/certs]

h3. WHY

Per MGDSRVS-188, MAS SSO will be migrated to Red Hat SSO. Existing references to MAS SSO URLS will become invalid.

h3.Resources
* Upstream code changes: https://github.com/redhat-developer/app-services-guides/pull/539/files

items.fromString:
h3. WHAT

The quick start we originally developed for Quarkus + Service Registry has the fairly broad title of [Using Quarkus applications with Kafka instances and Red Hat OpenShift Service Registry|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_service_registry/1/guide/7314d8c8-3c5b-457c-9c10-8817aa89b8f1] That guide also has a fairly basic short description on the documentation splash page.

As discussed and agreed with [~accountid:70121:962d1379-695f-42fd-9c27-520bf58346ef], now that we have service contexts (and also service binding) that enable users to generate connection configurations in a more automated fashion, we need to update our quick starts to more accurately reflect the use cases that they cover. These quick starts really cover the basic use cases of manually configuring connections using details that users collect in the console. 
h3. HOW

To more accurately reflect the use case covered by the Quarkus quick start for Service Registry, we need to update the following:
 * The title of the quick start in the source README file and in the Splash Page Manager
 * The short description of the quick start in the Splash Page Manager
 * The intro paragraphs of the quick start
 * Any links that reference the old title

h3. WHAT

The quick starts we originally developed for Quarkus and Node.js have the fairly broad titles of [Using Quarkus applications with Kafka instances|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_streams_for_apache_kafka/1/guide/04827d87-ed92-4ffd-a126-11fa13348eba] and [Using Node.js applications with Kafka instances|https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_openshift_streams_for_apache_kafka/1/guide/5b6badee-eaf3-4a10-b5ec-57dc6b94ec0f]. Those guides also have very basic short descriptions.

As discussed and agreed with [~accountid:70121:962d1379-695f-42fd-9c27-520bf58346ef], now that we have service contexts (and also service binding) that enable users to automatically generate connection configurations, we need to update the quick starts to more accurately reflect the use cases that they cover. These quick starts really cover the basic use cases of manually configuring connections using details that users collect in the console. 
h3. HOW

To more accurately reflect the use cases covered by the Quarkus and Node.js quick starts, we need to update the following:
 * The title of each quick start in the source README file and in the Splash Page Manager
 * The short description of each quick start in the Splash Page Manager
 * The intro paragraphs of each quick start
 * Any links that reference the old titles

items.fromString:
*WHAT*

Create UX mockups for the API Designer editor page.

 

*HOW*
 * Explore design options for the editor page and create UX mockups for it.
 * Some use cases/functionalities to address: 
 * Breadcrumbs
 * Description or metadata section can include the name of the design, type, version, etc. 
 * What information is shown for different design types (i.e. API or schema)? 
 * How does this information depend on how the user got to the editor page (i.e. did the user open a URL, a local file, or RHOSR artifact, etc.)?
 * How do we display this information (i.e. inline, expandable section, etc.)?


 * Display information about saved changes, when was the content last updated, any validation errors, etc.
 * What are the main actions that users can perform? What buttons do we need? What is the behavior of these buttons?
 * In which cases do we use a basic text editor? Which cases would have custom editors? 
 * What is the behavior of the editor? Do the changes save automatically? 
 * If we do have a save button, what will be its behavior? Does a modal open up? What will the modal consist of? What happens if the user clicks on any modal buttons? 


 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

 * What happens when the user clicks on any buttons that the modal might have?
 * Review the designs with stakeholders including the UX team and CCS.

 

*DONE*

Include the following where applicable:
 * Design documentation that includes information about design iterations, feedback, final or latest designs, etc.
 * UX team, content, and stakeholder review and acceptance. 

 

*Guidelines*

The following steps should be adhered to:
 * The final, proposed design ideas must align with PatternFly design components.
